newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania challenger seeks support to renew country.
newsitem.headline: Romania challenger seeks support to renew country.

text.p: The centrist challenging ex-Communist President Ion Iliescu urged supporters on Wednesday to muster their forces for an election victory to allow him to get on with the job of divesting Romania of its Communist past.

Academic Emil Constantinescu told his final campaign rally ahead of Sunday's run-off that Romanians were passing judgment on more than Iliescu's seven years in power since the 1989 upheaval that toppled Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

"We are fighting a regime that hijacked the (1989) revolution. But we have come a long way further than that," he told 4,000 backers jammed in the hall once used for Ceausescu's Communist Party congresses. Thousands more crowded around loudspeakers on a square outside.
"This is the end of a fight lasting 50 years. The sole source of imbalance in the country is Iliescu. We need to rid the country of imbalance for good."
His supporters vowed to gather at state television, where the contenders were holding the latest of several debates.

Constantinescu's comments were a recurring theme in the campaign and reflected the disappointment of liberals, who say ex-Communists manipulated the 1989 events to remain in power and block radical change.
The bearded geology professor trailed Iliescu by four points in the presidential poll's first round.
He has since won the support of former prime minister Petre Roman, the third-place finisher, who stood alongside him on the stage, beaming and thrusting his fist in the air.
The first opinion poll published before the run-off gave a 53 to 47 percent lead to Constantinescu. But it said a quarter of those asked were undecided. Surveys in Romania also tend to be erratic.

Iliescu has adopted a more aggressive tone in the second round, telling voters that Constantinescu is intent on bringing back exiled King Michael and restoring big landowners liable to take away their homes and livelihoods.
The opposition says defeat for Iliescu would complete the break with communism begun with the rout of his Party of Social Democracy in this month's parliamentary election.

Constantinescu's Democratic Convention promises to implement faster reforms, tax cuts and improved social benefits to close the growing gap in living standards with ex-communist states Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.

The role of the 1989 revolution has been repeatedly raised in the campaign as have opposition allegations that Iliescu was responsible for instigating later riots by miners in Bucharest targeting opposition parties and market reforms.
"It was a true revolution based on discontent aimed at dismantling an ailing system," Iliescu said of 1989 in the candidates' second television debate on Tuesday night.
"I don't know where Mr Constantinescu was then. I was in the middle. I could have been among those now in their graves."
Constantinescu retorted that the truth had yet to be told about why 1,500 people had been killed, mostly after Ceausescu was executed by firing squad west of Bucharest.
"We will find the truth we have been unable to find for seven years," he said. "Justice must run its course. Truth is like the air we breathe. Our future cannot be built on lies."
An array of parties has lined up behind Constantinescu, including former nationalist groups once allied with the president and most first-round also-rans.

The latest declaration of support came from the leader of 160,000 miners, not those who sparked the unrest of the early 1990s. Their leader, Marin Condescu, said he could swing up to a million votes to the challenger.
